"The man before you is Tobari Fushigorō, a pupil of this hall,"
Kondō presented him to Shichiri Kennosuke. "Tobari" was the stand-in, Katsura Kogorō.
"First, that you may learn the sword-habits of our school, I would have you try a bout with this man."
"Agreed."
Even as he nodded, Shichiri Kennosuke could not quite hide a look of doubt. Of a swordsman named Tobari Fushigorō he had never so much as heard.
And to look at him—was the man not a little fellow?
(Nothing much to him.)
Shichiri's face said as much.
At Kondō's hall it was the standing custom, whenever they called a man in from the Shintō Munen-ryū of the Saitō hall at Sanbanchō, to use for him the invented name "Tobari Fushigorō."
Presently old Kondō Shūsai, the hall's retired master, came out, and
"I am Kondō Shūsai,"
he said, with a nod to Shichiri Kennosuke, and tottered out to the center of the hall. He was there to judge the match.
Sixty-three.

He had the look of a farmer. Kondō, Hijikata, and Okita had all had their first lessons from the old man; Kondō and Okita had each received the full transmission, but Hijikata Toshizō alone had had no more than the mokuroku from him.
—Toshi's got the arm for it.
So Shūsai used to say.

—With live blades, even Isami would be in danger. But his is a mongrel style. Not the Tennen Rishin-ryū. Correct him as you will, he won't be corrected—so in the Tennen Rishin-ryū he's a mokuroku man, in his own self-taught style a full master, and that's measure enough for the likes of him.
He could be quite severe, then, in matters of school.
Now Katsura Kogorō rose to his feet.
Then Shichiri Kennosuke.
The two advanced to the center of the hall, took the nine-pace distance by the etiquette of the Kōbusho, exchanged bows, and, crouching, drew their shinai to the ready together.
Katsura, as has been said, is a little man. That little man let a shinai somewhat shorter than the common length float lightly above his head.
Shichiri Kennosuke, big-framed, was using a great shinai four shaku long. However one looked at it, the menace of his appearance was not Katsura's.
—Kondō.
Toshizō spoke low, his eyes on Katsura.
"He's going to lose, isn't he. That man—his hips ride far too high."
"Now you say it, there's no fighting spirit in him."

Fighting spirit—kigumi—means force of will, the fire of the spirit. Against the technique-worship of the other schools, the Tennen Rishin-ryū prized it above all. Indeed, with Kondō Isami it went further than swordsmanship: he applied it to the judging of men too, and had a way of settling a man's whole worth on nothing more than whether he had fighting spirit or lacked it.
"A clever little fellow, no more, after all,"
Toshizō whispered. To hear him, one would think he hated Katsura—the ally they had gone to the trouble of hiring—worse than Shichiri Kennosuke himself.
"But, Toshi,"
said Kondō,
"it won't end as a joke. If that fellow loses, you or Sōji will have to stand against Shichiri."
"With live blades, I don't mind. A man like Shichiri Kennosuke looks likely to haunt us for years to come; better to leave him with no legs to stand on."
"Grim things you say."
Just then, at the center of the hall, old Shūsai raised his hand and
—Three bouts to decide.
he proclaimed.

Shichiri Kennosuke sprang back into the low guard. The low guard is called the cunning one: rather than for attack, it is a stance well suited to drawing out an opponent's move. Naturally, the guard is a dark one.

Katsura, little man though he was, danced his point up and took a showy left overhead guard. There was brightness in the stance. A largeness, as of a man who had always walked in the sunlight, was in his body.
But an overhead guard from a small man. Shichiri, no doubt, judged it soft.
Shifting to the middle guard, he closed the distance in a rush, and pressing Katsura hard with his point,
"Yaa!"
he made to fall on the trunk. That faint lift of Shichiri's, at the very start, laid his wrist bare, and Katsura struck it with a speed the eye could not follow.
"Wrist!"
Old Shūsai's hand went up to Katsura.
Next, Katsura took the middle guard.

Shichiri Kennosuke took the right overhead, but his feet did not settle into a natural stance; in the old fencing way he planted them T-wise, in the shumoku stance, his stride wide. Well enough with a wooden sword or a live blade, but with the shinai it wanted suppleness.
(Country stuff.)
Even Toshizō thought so. The Kōgen Ittō-ryū sounds well enough, but in the end the field-smell of Bushū Hachiōji came off it plain to see.
In that, Katsura was another thing altogether. No strain in his body, and the shinai light. A great polished Edo school, sure enough.
Pat!—Shichiri's blade flew at Katsura's face; but Katsura, drawing his body back, in the same motion swept it up the ridge of his own sword, raised it high, stepped in, and struck the face.
(Deft.)
thought Toshizō.
But the blow was shallow, and Shūsai did not take it. In the Tennen Rishin-ryū, unless a blow bites to the bone it does not cut, and so is not counted.
Katsura stepped in further and struck the face three times running, but these too Shūsai did not take.

Next, Shichiri went for Katsura's face. But Katsura, in an instant, drove his hips forward, dropped his right knee to the boards, whirled the shinai and struck Shichiri's right flank—crack!—then, stepping out with his left foot, struck the left flank, and next, rising as he went, struck the wrist. Against Katsura's near-acrobatic handling of the shinai, Shichiri could do nothing at all. Last, whirling the shinai above his head, Katsura took him full across the side of the face.
"Face!"
Shūsai took the blow.
For the last of the three, Katsura, by the courtesy usual in such inter-school matches, yielded Shichiri a single wrist-touch and smartly drew his own shinai back.
(What an affected thing to do.)
The yielding was so transparent that it did not sit well with Toshizō.
"That is all."
Shūsai raised his hand.
When the match was over, Katsura, with an unfriendly face, put himself smartly to rights and made to slip away toward the far side of the hall.
"Toshi, see to the tea and sweets,"
said Kondō, in a fluster,
"I'll deal with Shichiri over wine and food. You take Katsura. And don't forget to have his palanquin ready for the road home."
"Hmph."
It did not please him, but Toshizō went out of the hall, and at the raised step of the entrance—
"Master Katsura,"
he called, stopping him.
"A place has been laid in another room; pray rest a while."
"No—I am in haste."

Katsura did not so much as turn. To put the standing of Katsura and Toshizō, at that moment, into today's terms: imagine the relation between the deputy director of a great general hospital and the locum of a little back-street clinic.
"But, Master Katsura,"
Toshizō caught his sleeve. Katsura turned—and started.
There were eyes there, and in them burned Toshizō's hatred.
Katsura was troubled.
(Why does this man look at me so?)
"Well, then,"
and Katsura followed Toshizō meekly. The place had been laid in old Shūsai's room.
Seating himself before the alcove post, Katsura found Toshizō making him a pointedly deep and reverent obeisance.
"I am Hijikata Toshizō, deputy master of this hall. I beg your acquaintance henceforth."
"And I yours."
Katsura returned the bow lightly.
Presently Kondō's wife, Otsune, brought in tea and sweets.
This too being a gloomy woman, she made the round of greetings but not one gracious smile.

Besides the tea and sweets, Otsune set before Katsura's knee a tray bearing paper and coin. Katsura took it with a practiced hand, tucked it into his breast, and after that, expressionless, lifted his teacup.
"Master Katsura,"
Toshizō said, offensively polite. In age and build the man was no different from himself.

"A little while ago I was given to see a splendid match; a rare feast for the eyes, I count it. Such skilled handling of the shinai, country fencing like the Kōgen Ittō-ryū or the Tennen Rishin-ryū could never come near."
"No, no."

"Thanks to you, the honor of this hall was upheld; but there is one thing I would ask, for my own instruction. Your exquisite handling of the shinai—would it go just the same if the weapon were a wooden sword, or a live blade?"
"That I cannot say."
Katsura was as unfriendly as ever. Toshizō pressed on:

"Whether the Tennen Rishin-ryū, or the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, or the Maniwa Nen-ryū, the fencing of Bushū and Jōshū was made for real fighting, and so, do what we will, in hall bouts we lose to the great schools of Edo."
"Is that so."
Such talk seemed to hold no interest for Katsura.
"Suppose,"
Toshizō said, fixing him with a stare,
"what would you say."
"To what?"
"If that had been no shinai but a live blade—could you have struck Shichiri Kennosuke so easily?"
"That I cannot say,"
said Katsura.
He would not be drawn. Go to teach at some little country school, and there was always one like Toshizō, who would ask,
—And in real fighting, how would it serve?
Katsura was used to it.
"But Master Katsura, suppose there were a ruffian here, and he fell upon you—what then?"
"Upon me?"
For the first time, Katsura smiled.
"I would run."
He seemed a man cut from wholly different cloth than Toshizō.
Kondō, in his own room, was seeing to Shichiri Kennosuke, having Otsune bring out wine and food.
Shichiri, when he had tossed off some ten cups one after another,
"Well, then? Come—"
"Wine, you mean?"
"No—the match."
Shichiri, with a sardonic face,
"This time I'd like to invite the worthies of your school to Hachiōji. Will you take me up on it?"
"Well, now—"
"Hachiōji wine is poor stuff, but as for the sword, the whole Hiruma hall will make you welcome enough. To tell the truth it was with that in mind that I asked for today's match. What do you say?"
"When I have talked it over with my pupils."
"Talk it over, by all means,"
Shichiri drained his cup at a gulp,
"but the stand-in—him I'll decline."
"Eh?"
"I'd not have you take me for a fool. Did you think I hadn't heard? I'm saying I'll not have you bring out some monster of a shinai-acrobat like that one."
"Is that so."
Kondō's face went hard. After that he said not a word. It was Kondō's way: when things turned against him, he fell silent, and silent, his face grew fearsome.
There Okita Sōji came in, to help the wine along.
"Sōji, this gentleman here,"
said Kondō,
"wishes to hold a match at Hachiōji. We shall have to take it up—but he says he'll have no shinai-acrobatics."
"Master Shichiri,"
Sōji turned to him and made a show of astonishment.
"You mean to say—with live blades? Now that's an ill notion. It would turn into a pitched battle outright. Before long they'll ban swordsmanship in all the Tama country."
"No,"
Shichiri said, but there was no keeping up with the boy.
"The day—which day is it to be?"
"The day I invite you, I'll fix in due course."
"But surely a pitched battle wants no day and no appointment."
"Sōji,"
Kondō, rather, was the flustered one.
"Stand down."
With a "Tcha," Sōji drew back, and in the corridor ran plump into Toshizō.
"Has Master Katsura gone already?"
"He's gone."
"A weary duty, I'm sure."
Okita was clowning. When this man began to clown, no good ever came of it.
"Hijikata, you're in no very good humor, are you. Master Kondō had just the same face on him—soured through and through."
"Is Shichiri still here?"
"He is indeed. More than here—now he's proposing not shinai but a pitched battle."
"Don't talk rot,"
Toshizō barked; but at once his face went grave. It was Shichiri, he might well do it. Out with it, he said—what was said?
"Oh, nothing much. In brief: he invites the whole of your school to Hachiōji, the day to be fixed later; not shinai, but live blades—"
"He said that?"
"Mm."
Okita Sōji drew in his pretty chin and nodded. Toshizō went out to the back of the hall.
There on the black earth the big man Harada Sanosuke lay stripped to the waist, his belly—broad as a village wrestler's—turned up to the sky.
This was the house-guest's daily habit. Across his belly ran a single straight scar, and because it ached now and then, as if remembering, he sunned it every day at a set hour.
"Harada,"
He got up with a "Hah."
"You said once, I think, that you'd like to try cutting a man down."
"I did say so."
An unfriendly man.

Fat he was, but fair-skinned, the shaved roots of his beard blue, and his eyes surprisingly cool. Yet a man short of temper beyond anything, so that even Kondō and Toshizō, in speaking with this house-guest, chose their words with great care.
"There's a chance of it—that very thing,"
said Toshizō, and picked up a bent nail.
It was Toshizō's way to fall at once to drawing maps. And so cunningly, they say, that anyone at all could see the very place before his eyes—a rare gift, surely, in a man of that day.
He drew one line, firmly:
"This is the Kōshū Highway."
"Mm."
"The Asa River comes down from the north."
"The Hachiōji station, then,"
Harada Sanosuke nodded.
Good, said Toshizō, and, making the lines steadily more intricate, at length pointed to a single spot.

"Here, Harada. By the night after next, get there and lodge. A cheap doss-house, grand in nothing but its name—the Edoya, it's called. I'll give Okita Sōji all the particulars; but this business—the young master—"
and, cocking his thumb,
"he's not to be told."
After that he told the same to the house-guests Tōdō Heisuke and Nagakura Shinpachi, and last called Okita Sōji and laid the plan out to him in full.
"Now then—you take them all to Hachiōji."
"And we put up at the Edoya, and wait for your signal before we fall on the Hiruma hall. But you, Hijikata—what will you do?"
"Me?"
Toshizō thought a moment.
"I set out."
"Now, this minute?"
"Aye. Before that Shichiri Kennosuke leaves this hall, I steal away ahead and go straight to Hachiōji."
"Well, I am surprised."
His face was not in the least surprised.
"And then—what will you do?"
"Pay a call at the Hiruma house."
"Pay a call?"
"War is the way of deception. Fall on the foe after he's made his quarrel ready, and the fight is an even thing. I go on ahead so as to let your men slip smoothly into that house."
"A strategist, no less."
Toshizō set out then and there.
To Hachiōji, thirteen ri.
On the way he passes before the Satō house at Hino. He goes straight by, of course.
Reaching Hachiōji, he will call at once at the Hiruma house.
That said, Toshizō did not imagine it a house one could call on by any ordinary procedure.
